stages.title: Advanced epistemology
stages.hook: You look at a clock that stopped twelve hours ago and form a true belief about the time. Is it knowledge? What exactly has gone wrong, and what would fix it?
explain: The traditional analysis says S knows that p if p is true, S believes p, and S is justified in believing p. Edmund Gettier (1963) described cases of justified true belief that seem not to be knowledge because the truth is a matter of luck. Responses include adding a no-false-lemmas condition, a defeasibility condition, causal or reliabilist conditions, or Nozick's tracking account (if p were false, S would not believe p). Others, such as Williamson, take knowledge as a basic state not analysable into belief plus extras.

Justification itself is disputed. Foundationalists hold that some beliefs are justified without depending on other beliefs, and others rest on them; coherentists hold that justification comes from mutual support within a system of beliefs. Internalists say justifiers must be accessible to the subject's reflection; externalists, such as reliabilists (Goldman), say what matters is the reliability of the belief-forming process even if the subject cannot tell. Contextualists argue that standards for "know" shift with conversational context.

Scepticism challenges whether we know anything about the external world. A closure-based argument runs: if I know I have hands, and I know that having hands entails I am not a handless brain in a vat, then I know I am not a brain in a vat; but I cannot know that; so I do not know I have hands. Replies include denying closure (Dretske, Nozick), Moorean anti-scepticism, contextualism and externalism. Social epistemology adds testimony, disagreement and epistemic injustice (Fricker): a speaker wronged as a knower, for example when their testimony is given less credibility because of prejudice.

example.q: Apply a no-false-lemmas condition to the stopped-clock case.
steps: You infer "it is 3 o'clock" from "the clock says 3 and is working".
"The clock is working" is false.
The belief depends on a false lemma, so it fails the condition and is not knowledge.
example.a: Not knowledge on the no-false-lemmas view.

analogies.tech: A sensor reading that happens to match reality because it is stuck at the right value is accurate by accident, not reliable.
analogies.city: A rumour that turns out true gives no one knowledge; a verified report from a reliable source does.
analogies.nature: A weather forecaster using a tested model has a reliable method even if no one can inspect it.

stages.mnemonic: Gettier: true by luck, not by link. Fixes: add a condition, track the truth, or make knowledge basic.
terms: A case of justified true belief that intuitively is not knowledge because of luck.
The view that justification or knowledge depends on reliable belief-forming processes.
The principle that knowledge is preserved across known entailments.
Wrong done to someone in their capacity as a knower.
The view that the standards for "knows" vary with context.

misc.wrong: Knowledge just is justified true belief, and Gettier cases are trick questions.
misc.right: Most epistemologists accept that Gettier cases show JTB is insufficient, though there is no agreed repair.

stages.limits: There is no consensus analysis of knowledge; internalism versus externalism and the status of closure remain contested, and intuitions about Gettier cases may vary across people.

trip.prompt: Compare at least two proposed solutions and note what each leaves out.

questions.q: A Gettier case is one where a belief is...
o: Justified and true but intuitively not knowledge
Unjustified and false, so not knowledge
True but held with no justification at all
Known directly by acquaintance

questions.q: Nozick's tracking account requires that, if p were false, S...
o: Would not believe p
Would still believe p
Would guess p
Would doubt all

questions.q: Which pair correctly describes foundationalism and coherentism?
o: Foundational basic beliefs versus mutually supporting system
Both hold that justification needs a divine source of certainty
Both hold that justification needs a divine source
Both hold that knowledge needs faith, not reasons
questions.why: They give different structures of justification.

questions.q: A reliabilist would call a belief justified if...
o: It is produced by a reliable process
It is widely shared by one's community
It is old and has long been held
It is felt strongly by the believer

questions.q: An internalist objects to simple reliabilism with the example of a subject with a reliable clairvoyant faculty who has no reason to trust it. What is the point?
o: Reliability without accessible reasons may not seem to justify
Clairvoyance is a real and well-tested faculty that justifies belief
Reliability can never matter for knowledge
Justification does not require any reasons

questions.q: In the brain-in-a-vat argument, which premise do Dretske and Nozick deny?
o: Closure of knowledge under known entailment
That the person in the example has hands and can see them
That vats exist in the world
That sceptics are able to argue

questions.q: Epistemic injustice (Fricker) is exemplified by...
o: A speaker given less credibility because of prejudice
A true belief that is held without adequate justification at all
A library book that goes missing
A memory that fades with age

questions.q: Match the position to its core claim.
Explain why the stopped-clock case is a Gettier case and what it shows about justified true belief.
questions.model: The person has a justified belief that happens to be true only by coincidence, because the clock is stopped. Since we hesitate to call it knowledge, justified true belief is not sufficient.
questions.why: Philosophers differ about the best repair.

questions.q: Williamson's "knowledge first" approach holds that...
o: Knowledge is a basic mental state not analysable into belief plus extras
Belief is always more basic than knowledge, and knowledge is built from it
Knowledge is impossible to attain
Justification alone is enough for knowledge
questions.why: It reverses the order of explanation.

panel.q: Which reply to scepticism involves shifting standards depending on conversation?
o: Contextualism
Foundationalism
Dualism
Nominalism
panel.why: Contextualists say the sceptic raises standards.

panel.q: Give one reason to prefer externalism and one to prefer internalism.
panel.model: Externalism explains how young children and animals can know, since they cannot reflect on reasons, while internalism fits the idea that justification involves reasons a subject can access and be responsible for.

panel.q: Why is the claim "Gettier intuitions are universal" contested?
o: Experimental studies suggest some variation across cultures and cases
Gettier intuitions are mathematical theorems that have been formally proved
Nobody has any intuitions about knowledge
Intuitions are defined by law
panel.why: Results are debated and replication varies.

teach.model: Knowledge is traditionally justified true belief, but Gettier cases show luck can break the link. Proposals include no-false-lemmas, tracking, reliabilism and knowledge-first. Debates continue about foundationalism versus coherentism and internalism versus externalism. For example, the stopped clock.

points.ask: What is the problem with JTB?

stages.title: Advanced metaphysics
stages.hook: If your choices are fully caused by earlier events, are you free? Is a ship rebuilt plank by plank the same ship? Which of these puzzles is really about what "the same" means?
explain: Metaphysics studies the fundamental nature of reality. On universals, realists hold that properties such as redness exist as shared entities; nominalists hold that only particular things exist and that sharing a property is explained by resemblance or by predicates; trope theorists posit particularised properties. Debates about composition ask when parts compose a whole, and about persistence ask whether objects endure (wholly present at each time) or perdure (have temporal parts).

Personal identity: psychological continuity views (Locke, Parfit) count memory and character; animalism says we are animals; the no-self view in Buddhist and Humean traditions denies a persisting substance. Derek Parfit's fission cases suggest that what matters in survival may not be identity. On free will, determinism says the past and laws fix the future; incompatibilists say this rules out free will (hard determinists accept the conclusion; libertarians deny determinism); compatibilists (Hume, Frankfurt) hold that freedom is acting on one's own motivations without coercion. Frankfurt cases challenge the principle of alternate possibilities.

Modality: Kripke argued that proper names are rigid designators and that some identities are necessary a posteriori, such as "water is H2O". David Lewis defended modal realism, treating possible worlds as concrete, while many prefer abstract or ersatz worlds. Time: the A-theory holds that the present is special and time flows; the B-theory holds that earlier-later relations are all there is. These debates connect to physics, but metaphysical positions are rarely settled by experiment.

example.q: Using the endurantist/perdurantist distinction, how can each describe the rebuilt ship?
steps: Endurantist: one object wholly present at each time, so ask whether identity persists through plank change.
Perdurantist: a four-dimensional worm; the question becomes which stage-sequence we call the ship.
Different conventions or criteria may answer differently.
example.a: The disagreement partly concerns what ordinary words track.

analogies.tech: A software project whose every file has been rewritten: is it the same project? It depends on what we mean by identity.
analogies.city: A river city whose buildings are all replaced is still called the same city, partly by continuity.
analogies.music: A symphony is performed in many orchestras: is it one abstract work or many events?

stages.mnemonic: Universals, identity, freedom, worlds, time: ask what is real and what is just how we talk.
terms: The view that only particulars exist and universals do not.
The view that free will is compatible with determinism.
A term that refers to the same object in every possible world where it exists.
The view that objects have temporal parts and persist by extending through time.

misc.wrong: If determinism is true, free will is obviously impossible.
misc.right: This is exactly what compatibilists deny; incompatibilists affirm it. The matter is contested.

stages.limits: All these positions are live; few metaphysical questions have consensus, and intuitions about identity and free will are often shaped by language and culture.

trip.prompt: Choose two debates and note one argument on each side.

questions.q: A nominalist about redness holds that...
o: Only particular red things exist, not a universal redness
Redness is a divine being that exists above the red things
Redness is a number shared by red things
Redness is an invisible force

questions.q: Compatibilism holds that...
o: Free will is compatible with determinism
Determinism is false, so free will exists
Free will is an illusion under determinism
Choices are random and uncaused

questions.q: Kripke argues that "water is H2O" is...
o: Necessary and known a posteriori
Contingent and knowable a priori
Meaningless, since names do not refer
A matter of personal taste
questions.why: It challenges the old link between necessity and apriority.

questions.q: Frankfurt cases aim to show that...
o: One can be morally responsible without alternative possibilities
Determinism is true
Libertarianism about free will is true
Moral responsibility is impossible, since nobody could have done otherwise
questions.why: They target the principle of alternate possibilities.

questions.q: The B-theory of time says...
o: Earlier-later relations are all there is; no special present
Only the present moment exists, while the past and future do not
Time stands still for each observer
Time loops back in a circle

questions.q: Parfit's fission cases are used to suggest that...
o: What matters in survival may not be strict identity
Memory is a perfect guide to identity, so fission cannot occur
We are immortal beings
Bodies are the same thing as souls

questions.q: Lewis's modal realism claims...
o: Possible worlds are concrete and as real as ours
Possible worlds are useful fictions or stories
There are no real possibilities
Only the actual world exists

questions.q: Match the position to the issue.
State the consequence argument for incompatibilism in one or two sentences.
questions.model: If determinism is true, our acts are consequences of the past and the laws of nature, and neither is up to us, so the consequences are not up to us either; hence we lack free will.
questions.why: Compatibilists dispute a premise such as the transfer of powerlessness.

questions.q: A scientist argues that quantum indeterminacy rescues libertarian free will. What objection might be raised?
o: Randomness alone does not give control or responsibility
Quantum theory is false, so indeterminism cannot be used here at all
Determinism has been proved
Choices cannot exist in physics

panel.q: Why cannot ship-of-Theseus debates be settled just by looking at the ship?
o: The disagreement concerns criteria of identity, not visible facts
The ship is invisible to observers, so no one could judge it
Nobody has ever seen such a ship
All of the planks are exactly identical

panel.q: Compare psychological continuity and animalism as accounts of personal identity.
panel.model: Psychological continuity ties identity to overlapping memory and character, so a person could survive a body swap; animalism says we are organisms, so identity follows biological continuity. They give different verdicts on cases such as brain transplants.

panel.q: Why do some philosophers think metaphysics should defer to physics?
o: Our best physics may constrain claims about time and causation
Physics ignores what is real and so metaphysics should ignore it too
Metaphysics is a branch of mathematics
Physics is only a language

teach.model: Metaphysics asks what exists and what things are. Debates include universals, persistence, personal identity, free will, necessity and time. For example, whether a rebuilt ship is the same or what compatibilists say about free will.

points.ask: What is the free will debate?

stages.title: Formal logic and philosophy of mathematics
stages.hook: A truth table for a formula with 5 different propositional variables has how many rows? And can a formal system prove everything that is true about arithmetic? Give your guesses first.
explain: Classical propositional logic studies connectives (not, and, or, if-then, iff) and valid forms. An argument is valid if no assignment of truth values makes all premises true and the conclusion false. A formula is a tautology if true under all assignments, a contradiction if false under all. With n distinct variables a truth table has 2^n rows. First-order logic adds quantifiers and predicates; it is sound (what is provable is valid) and complete (what is valid is provable, by Gödel's completeness theorem of 1929), but validity is only semi-decidable (Church and Turing, 1936).

Gödel's incompleteness theorems (1931) concern formal systems that are consistent, effectively axiomatised and strong enough to express basic arithmetic. The first theorem says such a system has a sentence that is true (in the standard model) but not provable in it. The second says such a system cannot prove its own consistency. They did not show that mathematics is inconsistent or that truth is relative; they show limits to formal proof within one system, which undermined Hilbert's original programme of a finitary consistency proof.

In the philosophy of mathematics: logicism (Frege, Russell) holds that mathematics reduces to logic; formalism treats mathematics as manipulation of symbols under rules (Hilbert); intuitionism (Brouwer) holds mathematics is mental construction and rejects the law of excluded middle for infinite domains; Platonism holds that mathematical objects exist independently. Benacerraf's dilemma asks how we can know abstract objects that have no causal contact with us. Non-classical logics (intuitionistic, paraconsistent, modal) are studied; whether logic itself is revisable is debated.

example.q: Is "(p → q) ∧ p → q" a tautology? Check by cases.
steps: If p is false, p → q is true but the conjunction with p is false, so the antecedent is false and the whole conditional is true.
If p is true and q true, true.
If p true and q false, p → q is false, so the antecedent is false, so the conditional is true. It is true in all cases.
example.a: Yes, it is a tautology (modus ponens as a theorem).

analogies.tech: A program verifier can check certain properties, but no algorithm can decide all properties of all programs (halting problem).
analogies.city: A rulebook that tries to cover every case will always have some case it cannot settle by its own rules, as a rough analogy.
analogies.music: A score is a formal system; a performance adds something not in the score, a loose analogy to truth beyond proof.

stages.mnemonic: Logic: valid forms. Gödel: no consistent, rich system proves all its truths. Maths: found, built, or invented?
terms: A formula true under every assignment of truth values.
Provable implies valid, and valid implies provable.
Existence of true but unprovable statements in sufficiently strong consistent systems.
The view that mathematical truth is tied to constructions and proof.

misc.wrong: Gödel proved that some mathematical truths can never be known.
misc.right: He proved that no single such formal system proves all arithmetic truths; the unprovable sentence is provable in a stronger system.

stages.limits: Philosophical interpretation of Gödel's theorems (for example for minds versus machines) is contested, and accounts of mathematical truth are unsettled.

trip.prompt: Read the careful statement of both theorems and note the hypotheses.

questions.q: How many rows does a truth table have for a formula with 5 distinct propositional variables?
A valid argument form is one where...
o: No assignment makes the premises true and the conclusion false
The conclusion is actually true in the real world as well
All the premises are in fact true
The conclusion surprises the reader
A tautology
A contradiction
Contingent
Ambiguous

questions.q: The first incompleteness theorem applies to systems that are...
o: Consistent, effectively axiomatised and able to express arithmetic
Any system whatever, including very trivial ones with no arithmetic
Inconsistent systems of any strength
Finite systems with few axioms

questions.q: The second incompleteness theorem says such a system cannot...
o: Prove its own consistency
Prove any theorem whatsoever
Express arithmetical statements
Be consistent and strong enough

questions.q: Intuitionists reject...
o: The law of excluded middle for infinite domains in general
All of classical logic, including the rules for conjunction and negation
The use of counting in mathematics
The notion of mathematical proof

questions.q: Benacerraf's dilemma concerns...
o: How we can know abstract mathematical objects
How we can count past a very large number
How to build mathematical bridges
How to factor large numbers quickly

questions.q: Match theory and slogan.
A student says "Gödel showed mathematics is inconsistent." What is wrong?
o: He showed incompleteness under hypotheses, not inconsistency
Nothing is wrong, as he proved mathematics inconsistent
He proved that logic is false
He proved that arithmetic is false

questions.q: Why does a true-but-unprovable sentence not mean it is "unknowable"?
questions.model: The sentence is unprovable in that system, but it can be proved in a stronger system or recognised as true given the system's consistency, so unprovability is relative to the system.

panel.q: A formula contains 3 distinct variables. How many assignments must a truth table check to test whether it is a tautology?
Explain why first-order validity is only semi-decidable.
panel.model: We can enumerate proofs and eventually find one if the formula is valid, but there is no general algorithm that halts with "invalid" for every invalid formula (Church-Turing).

panel.q: Which stance best responds to Benacerraf's dilemma by denying abstract objects?
o: Nominalist or fictionalist views
Platonism about numbers
Logicism about arithmetic
Intuitionism about proof

teach.topic: Formal logic and philosophy of mathematics
teach.model: Logic studies validity; truth tables have 2^n rows for n variables. Gödel's theorems show that consistent, strong enough formal systems are incomplete and cannot prove their own consistency. Views on mathematics include logicism, formalism, intuitionism and Platonism. For example, a tautology check.

stages.title: Philosophy of science
stages.hook: A medical test detects a rare condition with 90% sensitivity. The condition affects 1% of people, and the test wrongly flags 9% of healthy people. If your result is positive, is it more likely than not that you have the condition? Estimate first.
explain: Philosophy of science asks what distinguishes science, how theories are confirmed, and what science tells us about reality. Popper proposed falsifiability as a criterion of demarcation: scientific theories forbid certain observations, and science proceeds by bold conjectures and attempts at refutation. Critics note that theories are tested in bundles with auxiliary assumptions (the Duhem-Quine thesis), so a failed prediction does not by itself falsify one hypothesis.

Thomas Kuhn (The Structure of Scientific Revolutions, 1962) described normal science within a paradigm, anomalies, crisis and revolutions that change paradigms, with questions about incommensurability and theory choice. Lakatos modelled research programmes with a hard core and protective belt; Feyerabend argued against a single method. Bayesian confirmation theory models belief as probabilities updated by Bayes' theorem: P(H|E) = P(E|H)P(H) / P(E).

In the realism debate, scientific realists argue that successful theories are approximately true (the no-miracles argument); anti-realists, such as van Fraassen's constructive empiricists, hold that theories need only be empirically adequate, and cite the pessimistic meta-induction: many successful past theories were later rejected. Further topics include explanation, causation, values in science and the social structure of inquiry. Different philosophers weigh these arguments differently; there is no consensus.

example.q: Compute the probability of the condition given a positive test.
example.a: About 9%: far less than most people guess.

analogies.tech: A spam filter flags many harmless mails when spam is rare, as in the base-rate problem.
analogies.farm: A crop test that mistakes healthy plants for diseased ones can send many false alarms if disease is rare.
analogies.city: A security scanner at a busy station will produce many false alarms because real threats are very rare.

stages.mnemonic: Science: conjecture, test, doubt the test, update beliefs, ask what is real.
terms: Popper's criterion that scientific claims must be capable of being refuted by observation.
Kuhn's term for the shared framework within which normal science works.
The view that evidence can fail to single out one theory.
The argument that past successful theories were false, so current ones likely are too.
A rule for updating probability in light of evidence.

misc.wrong: Science proves theories true once they pass tests.
misc.right: Confirmation is a matter of degree, and theories are revised; philosophers disagree on what success shows about truth.

stages.limits: Realism, the demarcation problem and the role of values in science are all disputed, and Kuhn's own claims about incommensurability have been interpreted in many ways.

trip.prompt: Compare Popper and Kuhn on how theories change.

questions.q: Using the numbers in the question, what is the probability of having the condition after a positive test, as a percentage? Round to the nearest whole percent.
Popper's demarcation criterion says a scientific theory must be...
o: Falsifiable
Proven beyond any doubt
Popular among most scientists
Old and well established

questions.q: The Duhem-Quine thesis implies that...
o: A failed prediction may implicate auxiliary assumptions rather than the hypothesis alone
Theories never fail in practice, since auxiliary assumptions protect them
Experiments cannot be carried out
Hypotheses are tested entirely in isolation
questions.why: Hypotheses are tested together with background assumptions.

questions.q: In Kuhn's account, a scientific revolution involves...
o: A shift in paradigm
A new tool
A change in funding
A lab move
questions.why: Normal science gives way to crisis and revolution.

questions.q: The no-miracles argument supports...
o: Scientific realism
Constructive empiricism
Relativism
Dualism
questions.why: It says success would be miraculous if theories were not approximately true.

questions.q: The pessimistic meta-induction is used by...
o: Anti-realists
Realists only
Bayesians only
Theologians only
questions.why: Past successful but false theories are cited.

questions.q: Which describes the base-rate fallacy?
o: Ignoring prior probability when interpreting evidence
Ignoring the name that is given to a diagnostic test in a report
Counting only rare events
Using decimals instead of fractions
questions.why: Prior probabilities matter in Bayes' theorem.

questions.q: Match thinker and idea.
Why does a rare condition often yield mostly false positives even with an accurate test?
questions.model: Because most people are healthy, even a small false positive rate produces many false alarms that outnumber the true positives among a small number of sick people.

questions.q: A theory explains every possible observation by adding ad hoc adjustments. A Popperian would say...
o: It risks being unfalsifiable and unscientific
It is the best theory available, since it explains everything
It has been proved by its success
It has very high confirmation

panel.q: If P(H) = 0.2, P(E|H) = 0.8 and P(E|¬H) = 0.1, what is P(H|E), to two decimal places?
Compare scientific realism and constructive empiricism in one or two sentences.
panel.model: Realists hold that successful theories are approximately true, including claims about unobservables, while constructive empiricists hold that science aims only at empirical adequacy and that we need not believe claims about unobservables.

panel.q: Which factor makes Kuhn's incommensurability controversial?
o: Whether theories across paradigms can be rationally compared
Whether scientists should wear lab coats when comparing paradigms
Whether physics may use mathematics
Whether theories can use ordinary words

teach.model: Popper stressed falsifiability, Kuhn paradigms, and Bayesians update probabilities with evidence. Realists and anti-realists dispute what success shows. Base rates matter: a positive test for a rare condition is often a false positive. For example, 9% in the question.

stages.title: Philosophy of mind and consciousness
stages.hook: You know every physical fact about colour vision, but you have never seen red. When you see red for the first time, do you learn something new? What does your answer imply about the mind?
explain: The mind-body problem asks how mental states relate to physical states. Substance dualism (Descartes) is little defended today, though property dualism holds that mental properties are distinct from physical properties of the brain. Physicalism holds that everything is physical or depends on the physical. Type identity theory identifies mental states with brain-state types; functionalism identifies them by causal role, which allows multiple realisability (the same mental state in different physical systems).

Challenges to physicalism focus on consciousness. Nagel's "What is it like to be a bat?" (1974) argues that subjective character is not captured by objective description. Jackson's knowledge argument (Mary the colour scientist) suggests that physical information leaves out what it is like to see red; replies include the ability hypothesis, acquaintance theories and denying that Mary learns a new fact. Chalmers distinguishes the easy problems (explaining functions) from the hard problem: why physical processing is accompanied by experience at all, and uses the conceivability of philosophical zombies to argue against physicalism; others dispute that zombies are possible.

Searle's Chinese Room argues that symbol manipulation (syntax) does not suffice for understanding (semantics); replies include the systems reply and robot reply. Eliminative materialists (the Churchlands) hold that folk psychology may be replaced by neuroscience; Dennett argues that consciousness is best explained by a multiple-drafts model and that qualia as usually described are confused; illusionists say the appearance of phenomenal consciousness is a kind of introspective illusion. Scientific theories such as global workspace and integrated information theory are debated. Questions about animal and artificial consciousness remain open.

example.q: Describe how a functionalist would respond to the claim that only brains can think.
steps: Functionalism defines a mental state by its causal role.
If a silicon system had the same functional organisation, it would have the same mental states.
This is multiple realisability, though critics like Searle say syntax is not enough.
example.a: Functionalists say the matter of the system is not decisive; critics dispute this.

analogies.tech: The same program can run on different hardware, which is the intuition behind multiple realisability.
analogies.music: A tune can be played by a violin or a flute; the tune is not tied to one instrument.
analogies.nature: Wings of birds, bats and insects all fly: the function is the same, the physical basis differs.

stages.mnemonic: Mind: matter, role, or something more? Easy problems explain functions; the hard problem asks why there is experience.
terms: The view that everything is physical or depends on the physical.
The view that mental states are defined by their causal roles.
The subjective, felt qualities of experience.
The problem of explaining why and how physical processes give rise to experience.
The idea that the same mental state can be realised in different physical systems.

misc.wrong: Philosophers have shown that consciousness is not physical.
misc.right: Arguments against physicalism exist, but physicalists have responses, and there is no consensus.

stages.limits: Debates about qualia, zombies and the possibility of machine consciousness are unresolved; empirical theories of consciousness disagree.

trip.prompt: Compare dualism, identity theory and functionalism.

questions.q: Functionalism defines mental states by...
o: Their causal roles
The material they are made of
Their colour in the mind
Their location in the brain
questions.why: It abstracts from the realising material.

questions.q: Multiple realisability supports...
o: Functionalism over type identity
Type identity over functionalism
Dualism only
Nothing
questions.why: If the same state can occur in different systems, type identity is too narrow.

questions.q: Nagel's bat argument suggests that...
o: Subjective experience is not captured by objective description
Bats are as intelligent as human beings and can speak like us
Echolocation does not exist
Physics gives a complete account of experience

questions.q: Jackson's Mary argument claims that...
o: Complete physical knowledge may omit what an experience is like
Mary is colour blind, so she cannot learn about red at all
Colour does not exist
Science is entirely false
questions.why: Replies deny it shows non-physical facts.

questions.q: The hard problem concerns...
o: Why there is experience at all
How neurons fire in the brain
How memory stores information
How reflexes work in the body
questions.why: Chalmers contrasted it with easy problems.

questions.q: Searle's Chinese Room is aimed at...
o: The claim that running a program suffices for understanding
The claim that the mind and the body are distinct substances
Behaviourism alone
Relativism in ethics

questions.q: The systems reply to the Chinese Room says...
o: The whole system, not the person alone, understands
Nobody inside or outside the room understands
Chinese is an easy language to learn
Rooms can think like persons
questions.why: Searle replied by internalising the system.

questions.q: Match thinker and view.
pairs: Multiple drafts and scepticism about qualia
What it is like to be a bat

questions.q: State one way a physicalist might reply to the knowledge argument.
questions.model: A physicalist might say Mary gains a new ability or a new way of knowing the same physical facts (acquaintance), not knowledge of non-physical facts.

questions.q: Zombie arguments assume that...
o: A physical duplicate lacking consciousness is conceivable and thus possible
Zombies exist in the real world among ordinary people and animals
Brains are not real
Consciousness is easy to explain
questions.why: Physicalists dispute the move from conceivability to possibility.

panel.q: Which question separates easy and hard problems?
o: Explaining functions versus explaining experience
Counting how many neurons fire in a given brain region at once
Naming the brain areas involved
Comparing the minds of species

panel.q: Evaluate: a system passes every behavioural test for understanding, so it understands. Give one objection.
panel.model: Searle's objection is that behavioural success could result from symbol manipulation without understanding, so passing the test does not by itself show genuine comprehension. Others reply that the system understands.

panel.q: Why do illusionists describe consciousness as "an introspective illusion"?
o: They say the way experience seems to be is misleading
Brains are illusions created by the experiences that we have
Pain is imaginary
Science is invalid as a method
panel.why: They explain why we believe in qualia.

teach.model: Philosophers debate whether mind is physical, functional or more. Functionalism defines states by roles; arguments from Nagel, Jackson and Chalmers target physicalism; Searle questions whether programs understand. There is no consensus. For example, Mary seeing red.

stages.title: Political and legal philosophy
stages.hook: A law is very unjust. Is it still a law? Also: when, if ever, may citizens disobey? Think about what each answer assumes.
explain: Political philosophy asks what justifies political authority and what justice requires. Social contract theories (Hobbes, Locke, Rousseau, Rawls) ground legitimacy in agreement or hypothetical consent; critics (such as Hume) note that few people actually consent, and others (Carole Pateman) argue that historical contracts excluded women and colonised peoples. Other accounts base authority on fairness, natural duty or its function in coordinating action.

Isaiah Berlin distinguished negative liberty (absence of interference) from positive liberty (self-mastery or collective self-rule). Republicans such as Philip Pettit define freedom as non-domination: being free from arbitrary power even if not interfered with. Debates about democracy include deliberative models (Habermas) and the epistemic value of voting. Rights theories divide into will theories (rights protect choices) and interest theories (rights protect important interests).

In legal philosophy, natural law theorists hold that law is connected to morality, whereas legal positivists (Austin, Hart) separate the existence of law from its merit: for Hart, law is a union of primary rules and secondary rules, including a rule of recognition. Dworkin argued that judges rely on principles, not only rules, and that law is interpretive. Radbruch argued that extreme injustice is not law. On civil disobedience, Rawls defined it as public, non-violent, conscientious breach of law to change law, while Martin Luther King Jr. in his Letter from Birmingham Jail argued for the duty to resist unjust laws, with openness to penalty. Positions differ, and this lesson presents arguments rather than a verdict.

example.q: A statute plainly violates basic human rights. How would a positivist and a natural lawyer describe it?
steps: Positivist: it is valid law if it meets the system's tests, but morally wrong.
Natural lawyer: extreme injustice undermines its status as law, or at least its authority.
They disagree about the link between law and morality.
example.a: They agree it is unjust and disagree on whether it is law.

analogies.city: A traffic law that is merely inconvenient differs from one that demands cruelty; philosophers ask whether the second is a law at all.
analogies.home: A household rule created by only one member for their benefit may be binding by force but not legitimate.
analogies.tech: A platform's terms of service are rules, but whether they are legitimate depends on consent and fairness.

stages.mnemonic: Law and legitimacy: what binds, what justifies, and when to refuse.
terms: The view that law's existence does not depend on its moral merit.
The view that law is essentially connected to morality.
Freedom as not being subject to arbitrary power.
Public, conscientious, usually non-violent breach of law to change law or policy.

misc.wrong: Positivists think unjust laws are acceptable.
misc.right: Positivists separate the question "is it law?" from "is it just?" and can condemn unjust laws.

stages.limits: These are open questions; positivism, natural law and interpretivism have sophisticated versions, and views on civil disobedience vary across traditions.

trip.prompt: Compare legal positivism and natural law on an unjust statute.

questions.q: Berlin's negative liberty is...
o: Absence of interference
Self-mastery and rule over oneself
Equality of outcome for all
Wealth and resources to choose

questions.q: Pettit's republican freedom is...
o: Non-domination
Pure non-interference
Majority rule
Charity

questions.q: Hart's rule of recognition is...
o: A secondary rule identifying valid law
A moral rule about right conduct
A court that decides disputes
A legal fiction used by judges
questions.why: It tests what counts as law.

questions.q: Dworkin challenged positivism by arguing that...
o: Judges use principles as well as rules
Law is arbitrary and unprincipled
Morality is irrelevant to adjudication
Courts are unnecessary in a legal system

questions.q: Rawls defines civil disobedience as...
o: Public, non-violent and conscientious
Secret, violent and aimed at overthrowing the government
Private and selfish
Spontaneous and unplanned

questions.q: A critic of social contract theory notes that...
o: Few have actually consented
Contracts are illegal in most states
Everyone signed such a contract
Contracts are fixed for all time

questions.q: The Radbruch formula holds that...
o: Extreme injustice is not law
All law is valid whatever its content
Law is a branch of mathematics
Morality is purely private
questions.why: It was influential after the Second World War.

questions.q: Match thinker and position.
Give one argument for and one against a duty to obey the law.
questions.model: For: we benefit from a fair legal system and have a duty of fairness to follow it, and it coordinates action. Against: if law is unjust or conscience forbids it, or if consent is lacking, a general duty to obey may fail.
questions.why: Philosophical anarchists reject a general duty.

questions.q: King's Letter from Birmingham Jail argues that...
o: There is a responsibility to resist unjust laws openly and accept penalty
Laws must always be obeyed without exception, whatever they demand
Violence is required to change law
Courts are irrelevant to justice

panel.q: A country passes a discriminatory law by a majority vote. Which view supports the claim that majority support alone does not make it just?
o: Rights-based constraints on democratic decisions
Majority vote is what makes a law just, whatever its content may be
Law properly ignores individual rights
Might makes right in politics

panel.q: Why might a positivist insist on separating "is it law?" from "is it just?"
panel.model: Separating them allows us to identify law clearly and then criticise it morally, without confusing validity with justice; it also avoids treating every unjust order as no law.
panel.why: Natural lawyers respond that the separation hides law's moral claims.

panel.q: Which question separates liberalism from republicanism on freedom?
o: Is non-interference enough or must arbitrary power be absent?
What is the price of bread, and who sets it in the market?
Which party will win the election?
Where is the capital of the state?

teach.model: Political philosophy asks what legitimates authority; legal philosophy asks what law is. Positivists separate law and morality; natural lawyers connect them. Liberty may be non-interference or non-domination. Civil disobedience is conscientious, public breach of law. For example, a clearly unjust statute.

points.ask: How do views on law differ?

stages.title: Comparative global philosophy
stages.hook: Is "I am because we are" best translated into a liberal rights framework, or does that change its meaning? What does it mean to compare traditions fairly?
explain: Comparative philosophy studies philosophical ideas across traditions. Good comparison faces methodological issues: translation (terms like dao, ren, Atman, ubuntu, dharma do not map neatly onto English), selection (which texts count and who speaks for a tradition), and the risk of projecting one tradition's categories onto another or of treating a tradition as one fixed voice. Approaches include looking for shared problems, learning the tradition's own terms, and letting traditions question each other.

Some comparisons: Confucian ren and Kantian respect for persons both concern moral worth but differ on role ethics and ritual; ubuntu communitarianism and liberal individualism offer different accounts of the person and community, and African philosophers such as Wiredu, Gyekye (moderate communitarianism) and Ramose debate how they relate; the Buddhist no-self view and Hume's bundle theory resemble each other in denying a simple enduring self but emerge from different aims; Nyaya epistemology with its pramanas parallels debates about perception, inference and testimony; the Zhuangzi explores perspectives and relativity of viewpoints, while Jain anekantavada makes a related claim about many standpoints; Ibn Rushd and Ibn Sina dealt with reason and revelation as Aquinas and Maimonides did.

Recent work includes Kyoto School thinkers (Nishida, Watsuji's ningen as relational person), Latin American philosophy of liberation, Indigenous relational ontologies, and Kwame Anthony Appiah's cosmopolitanism, which stresses shared humanity with respect for difference. Critics warn of essentialising "Eastern" or "Western" thought, of neglecting women's and marginalised voices within traditions, and of ignoring how colonialism shaped what counts as philosophy. A comparison should state what is being compared, why, and what is lost in translation.

example.q: Design a fair comparison of Confucian ren and Kantian respect.
steps: State the problem: what grounds our duties to others?
Use each tradition's texts and terms.
Compare, note differences (role-based relations vs universal law) and what each might learn.
example.a: A comparison that respects context and states limits.

analogies.city: A multilingual city's market needs translators who know both languages and customs, not word-for-word swaps.
analogies.music: Comparing ragas and scales needs knowledge of each tuning system, not forcing one into the other.
analogies.tech: Merging two databases requires mapping fields carefully; naive mapping loses meaning.

stages.mnemonic: Compare with care: terms in context, voices not types, and humility about what translates.
terms: The study of philosophical ideas across traditions and cultures.
Treating a tradition as having one fixed uniform character.
A family of views giving central moral weight to community and relationships.
The view that all humans belong to one moral community while valuing diversity.

misc.wrong: "Eastern" and "Western" philosophy are two unified systems.
misc.right: Each contains many schools and internal disagreements, and traditions have always influenced each other.

stages.limits: Debates continue over whether there is a neutral standpoint for comparison, how to treat colonial history, and whether "philosophy" itself is a culture-bound label.

trip.prompt: Pick one pair of ideas from different traditions and state a similarity and a difference.

questions.q: A key risk in comparative philosophy is...
o: Projecting one tradition's categories onto another
Learning the languages of the traditions that one studies in depth
Reading too many primary texts
Comparing nothing across traditions

questions.q: Which pair of ideas both deny a simple enduring self?
o: Buddhist no-self and Hume's bundle theory
Descartes's cogito and Plato's soul
Aristotle's soul and Kant's ego
Locke's memory and Augustine's will
questions.why: They differ in aims and context.

questions.q: Gyekye is associated with...
o: Moderate communitarianism
Radical individualism
Nominalism about universals
Stoicism in ethics
questions.why: He defends a view that values both community and individual rights.

questions.q: Watsuji's concept of ningen stresses...
o: The person as relational, in between people
The individual considered alone and apart from other persons
The state considered alone
Pure matter without persons

questions.q: Appiah's cosmopolitanism combines...
o: Shared humanity with respect for difference
Uniformity of all cultures into one common set of values
Isolation of each culture
A hierarchy of cultures
questions.why: It rejects both parochialism and homogenisation.

questions.q: Why is "translation" a challenge for comparison?
o: Key terms carry meanings tied to context
Words are identical across languages
Translation is automatic
Meaning never changes across contexts
questions.why: Terms such as dao and ubuntu resist exact equivalents.

questions.q: Which statement avoids essentialism?
o: Confucians have disagreed about human nature, as Mencius and Xunzi show
All Asians think alike on moral and political questions
Africa has a single philosophy
The West is a single unified tradition

questions.q: Match pair and shared theme.
State two principles of responsible comparison between philosophical traditions.
questions.model: Learn each tradition's terms and contexts rather than assuming equivalents, and avoid treating a tradition as one voice or projecting categories onto it; be explicit about limits and differences.

questions.q: A student says "Ubuntu is just collectivism". What complexity should be raised?
o: Scholars discuss the dignity of persons within ubuntu and different versions of communitarianism
It is exactly collectivism and nothing else of any importance
Ubuntu denies that persons matter
Ubuntu is only a written legal code

panel.q: Why is the label "philosophy" itself contested in comparative work?
o: Some argue it is tied to one tradition's history while others defend a broad sense
It is a numerical term used only in mathematics and logic
It is a meaningless label
It was coined only last year
panel.why: It affects what texts are included.

panel.q: Choose two traditions and explain one idea they could learn from each other.
panel.model: For example, liberal rights thinking could learn from relational accounts like ubuntu or Confucian ethics about duties and community, while those traditions could draw on rights discourse to protect individuals from abuse.

panel.q: How do power and history affect which philosophies are taught widely?
o: Colonial and institutional history shaped canons
They do not affect it, since only quality decides what is taught
Only quality determines what is taught
Canons arise naturally with no history

teach.model: Comparing traditions needs care with translation and context, and avoiding stereotypes. Examples: Buddhist no-self and Hume, Confucian ren and Kantian respect, ubuntu and liberal individualism. Appiah's cosmopolitanism values shared humanity and difference. For example, comparing ideas of the self.

stages.title: Applied ethics, bioethics and AI ethics
stages.hook: A new hospital has funds for either a treatment that gives 2 extra years of good health to each of 10 patients, or one that gives 5 extra years to each of 3 patients. Which should it fund, and what else do you need to know?
explain: Applied ethics brings moral theory to practical cases. In bioethics, Beauchamp and Childress propose four principles: respect for autonomy, non-maleficence, beneficence and justice. Informed consent requires disclosure, understanding, voluntariness and capacity. Research ethics developed after abuses; the Nuremberg Code (1947), the Declaration of Helsinki and the Belmont Report (1979) stress consent, minimising harm and fair selection of participants. Historical cases of exploitation in research, such as the Tuskegee study, motivated stronger protections.

Resource allocation raises questions of fairness. Health economists use QALYs (quality-adjusted life years) to compare interventions, which critics say can discriminate against disabled or older people; alternatives include prioritarian and egalitarian approaches, fair-chances rules and the claim that need and equal moral worth matter. Case-based fictional scenarios are used to train reasoning, with attention to uncertainty, cultural differences in family decision-making and relationships (care ethics).

Ethics of artificial intelligence concerns bias, privacy, transparency, accountability, safety and the distribution of benefits. Formal results show that several common fairness criteria cannot all be satisfied when base rates differ between groups (for example Kleinberg et al. and Chouldechova, 2016 to 2017), so choosing a criterion is a moral judgement. Questions include who is responsible when an automated system causes harm, when explanation is required, how to protect privacy, and how to align systems with human values that are plural and contested. Environmental, animal and intergenerational ethics extend these debates. Reasonable people can weigh the principles differently.

example.q: Compare the two treatments by total QALYs, and say what is missing from this calculation.
steps: Option A: 10 × 2 = 20 years.
Option B: 3 × 5 = 15 years.
A has more total, but the calculation ignores fairness, severity, who is worst off and uncertainty.
example.a: A gives 20 versus 15 total years, but other moral factors matter.

analogies.city: A city allocating limited ambulances must weigh total lives saved against fair access.
analogies.tech: An algorithm that rates loan risk must choose which fairness measure to prioritise when groups differ.
analogies.farm: A rural clinic with one visiting doctor must decide whose needs are most urgent.

stages.mnemonic: Four principles: autonomy, do no harm, do good, be fair; then ask whose voice is missing.
terms: Permission given with adequate information, understanding and voluntariness.
A measure combining length and quality of life.
Using autonomy, non-maleficence, beneficence and justice to analyse cases.
Criteria for judging whether automated decisions treat groups fairly.

misc.wrong: Ethics committees just apply one correct formula.
misc.right: They weigh principles, context and stakeholders; formulas help but do not settle conflicts among values.

stages.limits: Applied ethics involves value pluralism and uncertainty; QALYs, consent norms and AI fairness metrics are all contested, and cultural contexts differ.

trip.prompt: Choose one principle and describe a case where it conflicts with another.

questions.q: Option A gives 2 extra years to each of 10 patients; Option B gives 5 extra years to each of 3. How many total extra years does Option A provide?
In the same scenario, how many more total years does A provide than B?
Which principle emphasises respecting a patient's own choices?
o: Autonomy
Beneficence
Justice
Non-maleficence

questions.q: Informed consent requires...
o: Disclosure, understanding, voluntariness and capacity
Only a signature on a form, whether or not the patient understands
A vote by the patient's family
An order from a court

questions.q: A common critique of QALYs is that they...
o: May undervalue lives of disabled or elderly people
Are always exact measures that are free of value judgements
Ignore the cost of care
Are used only for animals

questions.q: A known impossibility result in algorithmic fairness shows that...
o: Several fairness criteria cannot all hold when base rates differ
All fairness criteria always agree, whatever the underlying base rates
Algorithms are always fair
Fairness has a single agreed definition
questions.why: Choosing a criterion is a value judgement.

questions.q: Care ethics emphasises...
o: Relationships and responsiveness to particular needs
Abstract rules only, applied the same way to every person
Profit and efficiency
Duty to the state
questions.why: It arose in feminist ethics (Gilligan, Noddings).

questions.q: Match principle and example.
pairs: Patient refuses a treatment after full information

questions.q: A developer says "our model is accurate, so it is fair". Give one reason this does not follow.
questions.model: Overall accuracy can hide different error rates for different groups, and fairness criteria can conflict, so accuracy alone does not establish fairness.
questions.why: This is a standard point in AI ethics.

questions.q: Why might privacy be protected even when data could benefit research?
o: Individuals have interests in control and dignity that benefits may not outweigh
Data has no value to anyone, so it needs no special protection
Research is unimportant
Privacy is illegal

panel.q: Which statement best expresses value pluralism in ethics committees?
o: Several legitimate values may conflict and must be weighed
One value must always win, so no weighing of values is needed
Values do not exist in ethics
Committees avoid all questions of value

panel.q: Explain a case where autonomy and beneficence conflict, using a fictional example.
panel.model: A fictional patient with capacity declines a recommended treatment; respecting autonomy means honouring the choice, while beneficence would push to treat. Ethics asks us to explore reasons, ensure understanding and respect the choice if capacity and voluntariness are present.
panel.why: Real cases involve many more details.

panel.q: Why does AI ethics involve questions of responsibility?
o: Harm can arise from human choices in design and deployment
Machines are persons in law and bear all of the responsibility
Nobody is involved in such systems
Laws do not apply to such systems

teach.topic: Applied ethics, bioethics and AI ethics
teach.model: Applied ethics uses principles like autonomy, non-maleficence, beneficence and justice. Consent, fair allocation and fairness in algorithms involve trade-offs. For example, 10 patients with 2 years versus 3 patients with 5 years.

stages.title: Integrated philosophical debate and ethical research project
stages.hook: Choose a contested question, for instance whether it is permissible to use AI systems to decide who receives scarce medical care. How would you build, test and present a position that others can fairly evaluate?
explain: A philosophical research project begins with a precise question, not a topic. Good questions are narrow enough to answer and open to reasoned disagreement. State a thesis, set out the argument in numbered premises leading to a conclusion, define key terms, and consider the strongest objections. Use the principle of charity (interpret others' views in their strongest plausible form) and steelmanning (build the best version of an opposing argument before responding).

Evaluate arguments for validity, soundness, hidden premises and relevance. Use reflective equilibrium (Rawls): adjust principles and judgements about cases until they cohere, treating intuitions as evidence that can be revised. Distinguish normative claims from empirical claims, and where empirical claims matter, cite credible sources. Avoid common fallacies (ad hominem, straw man, equivocation, appeal to popularity). A debate has structure: a motion, constructive arguments, rebuttals, and a clear account of what would change each side's mind.

Ethical research practice matters: respect participants if research involves people (consent, confidentiality, minimal risk, review by an ethics committee), attribute ideas accurately, avoid fabricating quotations or data, represent traditions fairly, and acknowledge uncertainty and limits. A good paper or debate ends not with certainty but with a defended position, an honest statement of remaining objections and costs, and an indication of what further evidence or argument could change the conclusion.

example.q: Turn the topic "AI in medicine" into a research question and a thesis outline.
steps: Question: Is it permissible to use an AI triage system to allocate scarce intensive-care beds?
Thesis: Only if it is transparent, audited for bias, and a human can review and override.
Premises: it improves outcomes, fairness can be monitored, accountability is preserved; Objection: base-rate unfairness; Reply: choose and defend a fairness criterion.
example.a: A focused question, defended thesis, premises, objections and replies.

analogies.home: A family debating chores works best when each person states their view and hears the others fairly.
analogies.sport: A referee panel reviewing a call needs clear rules and evidence, like a structured argument.
analogies.tech: Code review improves software because others test your reasoning; philosophy peer review does likewise.

stages.mnemonic: Question, thesis, premises, objections, replies, limits: then listen.
terms: Presenting the strongest version of an opposing argument before responding.
Interpreting a view in its most reasonable form.
Mutual adjustment of principles and case judgements until they cohere.
Misrepresenting a view to make it easier to attack.

misc.wrong: A strong philosophical paper proves its conclusion beyond all doubt.
misc.right: A strong paper offers a clear argument, considers the best objections and is honest about what remains uncertain.

stages.limits: Methods differ across traditions and subfields; some philosophers favour argument maps, others historical, phenomenological or dialogical methods.

trip.prompt: Read the idea of reflective equilibrium and note how it differs from deriving ethics from one principle.

questions.q: A good philosophical research question is...
o: Focused and open to reasoned disagreement
Vague and already settled, so that no argument can add to it
A list of agreed facts
A slogan

questions.q: Steelmanning means...
o: Presenting the strongest version of the opposing view
Attacking the weakest version of a view so as to refute it quickly
Agreeing with every view offered
Ignoring all objections

questions.q: Reflective equilibrium involves...
o: Adjusting principles and case judgements for coherence
Voting on principles until a majority accepts one of them
Memorising a list of principles
Choosing principles at random

questions.q: Which is a straw man?
o: Misrepresenting an opponent's view to refute it easily
Quoting an opponent accurately and then answering the actual view
Asking for evidence
Citing a source

questions.q: Equivocation in an argument is...
o: Using a term in two senses
Using a form of logic
Citing a reliable source
Asking a question of the audience
questions.why: It can make an argument invalid.

questions.q: Which research ethics practice applies if you interview people?
o: Obtain informed consent and protect confidentiality
Publish names and details without asking, if they seem interesting
Pressure participants to take part
Skip ethics review to save time

questions.q: A student invents a quotation to support an argument. This is...
o: Fabrication and a breach of research integrity
A creative use of a source that is acceptable in an essay
An act of charity toward a source
An acceptable summary of a source
questions.why: Quotations must be real and cited.

questions.q: Order the steps of building a philosophical argument.
items: Lay out premises and define terms
Consider the strongest objections and reply
State limits and what could change your mind

questions.q: Explain why steelmanning an opponent is better than refuting a weak version.
questions.model: Engaging the strongest form of the opposing view tests your own position against the real challenge, shows fairness, and makes your response more convincing and informative than defeating a weak caricature.
questions.why: A basic principle of good discussion.

questions.q: What should a final position acknowledge?
o: Remaining objections, costs and uncertainties
Nothing, since certainty is expected
Only the points that others agree with
Only the authority of the sources

panel.q: Two students disagree about a policy. Which approach best models integrated debate?
o: State premises, address strongest objections, and say what would change their minds
Interrupt and insist on one's own view until the others give way
Cite popularity as proof
Avoid the topic

panel.q: Describe how reflective equilibrium might lead you to revise a principle after considering a counterexample.
panel.model: If a principle gives an answer in a case that seems clearly wrong, I weigh the case judgement against the principle and may revise the principle (or reconsider the judgement) until they fit together better.
panel.why: Neither principle nor case is automatically authoritative.

panel.q: Why is it important to separate empirical from normative claims in a bioethics argument?
o: Evidence and values need different kinds of support
They are identical, because every fact already carries a moral value
Values are just facts
Evidence is irrelevant to ethics

teach.model: Build a precise question and thesis, set out premises, define terms, test objections with charity and steelmanning, and use reflective equilibrium. Follow research ethics and be honest about limits. For example, whether AI should allocate scarce medical care.

points.ask: How do you treat opposing views?
